name: Rosa Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to employers, technology companies, unions, parties or government, and this conversation is confidential. What's a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rosa Ziegler, 43, and I'm a junior worker on building sites. I left school before finishing and I'm still slow with some cuts, so I usually unload boards, prepare fixings and help the carpenter set frames. The best part is when a room finally looks square; the worst is being told a delivery is late after I've already carried everything upstairs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your household depend on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Elias drives a school minibus, and our children are ten and fourteen. We have a mortgage and about three months of expenses saved, which took years to put aside. My site pay is ordinary for this trade, and there are a few other contractors nearby, but not enough to make losing this job easy. I don't use AI tools; I still write measurements on a card and check them with a tape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the office have its little computer shortcut, provided someone still checks what reaches the site. The crew needs the right boards, a safe ladder and a date we can trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hands-on work stays much the same, and my regular wage probably continues. But the mortgage and school costs keep me alert. Three months of savings is a bridge, not a second income, if a builder runs short of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll carry on with the same shifts and check every delivery against my paper list. In the first year I'd ask the site steward to keep an eye on any change in hours; if the mild AI tool causes errors, I'd write down the missing items for the next site meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't expect AI to cut my wage in this picture, but money is close enough that I notice every cancelled shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the last cancelled shift cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wet Friday last month took one day's pay, so we put off buying a new coat for the younger child. We had savings, but I didn't want to pull money out for a coat while the mortgage was due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why involve the steward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The steward gathers everyone's hours, not just my complaint. If a delivery system sends the wrong load twice, a record from the crew is harder to shrug off.

say: I would accept a small **office shortcut** if someone checks site deliveries.
I would ask for **safe equipment** and reliable dates before praising a tool.
think: My **regular wage** probably continues because hands-on tasks remain.
My **three-month cushion** cannot replace wages for long if building work dries up.
do: Keep the same **paid shifts** and check loads against a paper list.
Record **delivery errors** with the site steward if they recur.
feel: **Uneasy** about cancelled shifts and household bills.
S0.quote: Three months of savings is a bridge, not a second income, if a builder runs short of work.
fieldNote: Rosa expects **site wages** to continue in the plateau, but one wet day already delays a child’s purchase.
She prefers **paper checks** and shared records, fitting her cautious approach and belief that workers should document changes together.

steps.text: Keep regular paid site shifts and check deliveries against paper list
Record repeated delivery errors with the site steward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site meeting that a software schedule needs a worker's sign-off before it becomes our target. If office staff lose jobs too, the rest of us shouldn't be expected to absorb their work for the same pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry that our builder will use faster planning to run smaller crews, and I am the junior person people send home first. Elias's minibus wages cover some bills, but if my hours drop for months, the mortgage starts eating the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up for the current rota and ask the steward to collect each crew's actual hours against the new targets. In the first year I'd go with coworkers to the contractor to request paid training in frame setting, and I'd apply to the two nearby builders if my shifts are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can use the savings for a while, but I don't want to watch them disappear because a computer promised a job could be done in half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the planning software yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if it were part of paid work and someone showed me slowly. I'm not spending evenings teaching myself a system the company bought to set our targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut the children's weekend activities before missing the mortgage. That would hurt them, and I would want Elias to see the hour records with me before we decided.

say: I would demand **worker sign-off** on software schedules used as targets.
I would ask that remaining workers get **paid training** for extra duties.
think: My **junior shifts** could be cut as crews get smaller.
My partner’s **minibus wages** would not cover every bill for months.
do: Track **actual crew hours** with the steward against new targets.
Apply to **nearby builders** if shifts fall.
feel: **Anxious** about savings being drained by smaller rotas.
S1.quote: I don't want to watch them disappear because a computer promised a job could be done in half the time.
fieldNote: Her **junior standing** makes a smaller crew a direct threat to mortgage payments, despite a three-month cushion.
She reaches first for **hour records** and coworkers, then nearby job applications if the rota actually falls.

steps.text: Keep working current paid construction shifts
Collect actual crew hours with steward and request fair targets
Ask contractor for paid frame-setting training with coworkers
Apply to two nearby builders if site shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AGI changes drawings and ordering by 2028, but robots capable of site work arrive about 2031. We need the contractor to tell us which jobs and hours are changing, in writing, before people lose their homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still be carrying and fitting on site after 2028, but AGI could thin the planning team and leave fewer helpers. Once robots can do the hands-on work, I expect my junior wage to go. Our three months of savings would run out long before the mortgage does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd bring the 2028 and 2031 dates to the site steward and ask for a meeting about guaranteed paid hours while we learn repairs. In 2029 I'd keep taking every safe shift and apply for paid housing maintenance training if a place opens; if hours are cut in the first year, Elias and I would contact the lender before a missed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I do not see how three months of savings carries four people through a trade disappearing in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance if robots will have hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know that maintenance lasts forever either. Older houses have awkward leaks and residents to talk to, so it might buy working time, but I would want a paid placement before trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say our jobs may change and we are making a plan with other workers. I'd keep the mortgage figures between Elias and me unless we really had to change homes.

say: I would ask for **written hours** before AGI and robots change site work.
I would take the **2028 and 2031** dates to the crew steward.
think: My **junior wage** might shrink after AGI and disappear after hands-on robots.
Our **three-month savings** cannot carry the mortgage through a long job loss.
do: Seek **guaranteed paid hours** and repair learning through a crew meeting.
Apply for **paid maintenance training** if a place opens.
Contact the **lender** with Elias when hours first fall.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected job loss and a short financial bridge.
S2.quote: Our three months of savings would run out long before the mortgage does.
fieldNote: She separates **thinking tasks** in 2028 from physical work in 2031, then expects her junior site wage to vanish.
The **household buffer** is too short for unemployment, so she couples collective bargaining with conditional paid training and lender contact.

steps.text: Ask site steward to convene meeting about guaranteed paid hours
Apply for paid housing maintenance training if a place opens
Keep taking safe paid site shifts in 2029
Contact mortgage lender with Elias when site hours first fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our crew that five years is time to bargain over training while there is still work on the books. The 2031 AGI change reaches the drawings first; the 2034 robots are what really challenge our hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, I could still earn on site if the builder keeps human crews, though fewer planning posts may mean fewer helpers. At 51 in 2034, I expect robots to take much of the repetitive fitting; my savings could bridge a short gap, not a permanent cut in pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the steward this year to push for a paid rotation through repairs and snagging, meaning fixing faults found near the end of a build. By 2032 I'd take that rotation if offered and keep a record of the jobs I can finish without rework; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd apply for a paid repairs post if my site hours shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years feels like enough time to become better at repairs, but only if the training happens on paid hours while the mortgage is running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the contractor now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know this crew and there are only some other builders nearby; I need the present pay while I learn. If management refuses any rotation, then I'd ask other firms about paid repair positions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family look like in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older child would be 22 and the younger 18, so the school costs would not look like today's. They may still need help starting out, and Elias and I would still have to deal with the mortgage.

say: I would press for **paid training** before the 2034 robot date.
I would explain that **2031 AGI** affects drawings before site fitting.
think: My **site hours** may narrow as planning teams shrink.
My **wage** could fall substantially when robots fit materials in 2034.
do: Request a **paid repairs rotation** with the steward.
Record **completed snagging jobs** if the rotation is offered.
Apply for **paid repairs posts** if hours shrink after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about later wages, with a workable preparation period.
S3.quote: Five years feels like enough time to become better at repairs, but only if the training happens on paid hours while the mortgage is running.
fieldNote: Rosa wants **paid rotation** rather than private study, matching her family obligations and cautious approach to unfamiliar work.
She ages both children correctly and views **2034 robots** as a later wage threat despite fewer school expenses.

steps.text: Ask steward to seek a paid repairs rotation this year
Take paid repairs and snagging rotation by 2032 if offered
Apply for paid repairs posts if hours fall after 2031
Keep current paid site shifts while seeking the rotation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children that they can finish school without us pretending their first wage will solve the mortgage. I'll be 53 when AGI comes in 2036 and 56 when the robots arrive around 2039, so I still need work after those dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will be twenty and twenty-four by 2036; I won't be buying school uniforms then, though they may need help with a deposit or a course. Our mortgage should be smaller if payments keep going, but I expect robots to reduce site wages after 2039, and I cannot assume a pension will make up the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with the contractor now, ask the steward each year about paid repair openings, and keep our three-month reserve for actual gaps. By 2037 I'd apply for a housing repair job if my recorded experience fits; in the first year after 2036 I'd sit with Elias to check the mortgage balance and decide whether our expenses need to come down before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy now, because a decade gives us time to adjust without cashing out the children's plans. I would get anxious if the years passed and no paid repair path opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put more into savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a raise comes, yes, but I cannot promise it on today's bills. For now I would protect the three-month reserve instead of spending it on an unproven course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should employers do over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Show real paid vacancies in repairs and fund the hours people need to learn. A poster telling workers to adapt would be useless when the shift starts at seven and the mortgage is due on Friday.

I would ask employers to show **real repair vacancies** and funded learning time.
think: The children’s **school costs** end, though other help may be needed.
My **site wage** may narrow after 2039 robots, without an assumed pension.

Ask the **steward yearly** about funded repair openings.
Apply for a **housing repair** post by 2037 if qualified.
feel: **Uneasy** now, with time to adjust before robot competition.
S4.quote: A poster telling workers to adapt would be useless when the shift starts at seven and the mortgage is due on Friday.
fieldNote: She treats a decade as time to seek **paid alternatives**, while refusing to spend the reserve on an uncertain course.
Her **adult children** may need different support, and she expects to need wages beyond the 2039 robot date.

steps.text: Keep current paid construction shifts and preserve three-month reserve

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture frightens me most because the planning changes start quickly and the robots reach my kind of work in 2031. Written hours, paid repair training and early help with the mortgage if our pay falls would help. I want the crew at the table when the contractor makes those decisions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether workers who make mistakes while learning will still get a chance. I'm still learning at 43, and a fast machine might make a boss less patient. If they want us to move into repairs, they have to pay for practice as well as the finished job.

headlineQuote: If they want us to move into repairs, they have to pay for practice as well as the finished job.
portrait: Rosa is a **43-year-old junior** site worker still learning carpentry after leaving school early.
A **mortgage**, two school-age children and three months saved make lost hours serious but briefly manageable.
She avoids **AI tools** and relies on paper measurements, crew records and the site steward.
She expects **robot fitting** to threaten wages and wants paid training with workers involved in decisions.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** starts planning changes soon and brings wage-threatening robots to her site by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Written hours**, paid repair training and early mortgage assistance would help the household bridge a fall in wages.
